findings.title: Invite codes use non-cryptographic RNG and small keyspace
findings.description: create_invite() generates the code with random.randrange, which is a Mersenne Twister PRNG that is not cryptographically secure and can be predicted if its internal state is inferred. Combined with only 6 hex characters (16^6 ≈ 16.7M possibilities) and no rate limiting on accept_invite(), an attacker can brute-force valid codes and join a household to gain access to shared financial data. Should use the `secrets` module (e.g. secrets.token_hex) and consider a longer code.

findings.title: Invite codes are never consumed, allowing unlimited reuse by different users
findings.description: The invites table has a used_at column, implying single-use semantics, but accept_invite() never checks or sets it. Once a code is created it remains valid forever and can be used by any number of distinct users to join the household (the only check is 'already a member' for the same user), not just the one intended invitee. This defeats the purpose of a controlled invite and lets a leaked/guessed code be reused indefinitely.

findings.title: No handling of invite code collisions
findings.description: code is generated with 16^6 possibilities and inserted directly with no uniqueness check or retry loop. Since `code` is the PRIMARY KEY, a collision with an existing (especially still-unused/unexpired) invite will raise an unhandled sqlite IntegrityError instead of being retried or surfaced as a HouseholdError, causing create_invite() to crash for the owner.

findings.title: Invite codes never expire
findings.description: created_at is recorded but accept_invite() never checks how old an invite is. Codes remain valid indefinitely, which increases the exposure window for guessing/brute-forcing and for accidental reuse of codes shared long ago.

findings.title: No test that an invite code cannot be reused by a second, different user
findings.description: test_member_cannot_accept_twice only verifies that the *same* user cannot accept twice; it does not test the actual intended single-use invariant (that once carol has used the code, a different user, e.g. bob, should not be able to join with the same code). Because accept_invite() never marks codes as used, this real bug is not caught by the test suite.
